introduction-the-grand-illusion.core: Every process believes it has a large, private, contiguous address space starting at zero. In reality the kernel maps virtual pages to scattered physical frames on demand, shares identical pages (libraries, copy-on-write after fork), uses free RAM as page cache, moves rarely used pages to swap, and reclaims or kills under pressure. Virtual memory provides isolation, convenience and efficiency, and explains why 'used memory' numbers are so confusing.

first_principles.problem: free shows 'used' at 95% and engineers panic, though the system is healthy.
truths: Free RAM is used as cache.

analogy.title: A hotel that promises every guest a whole floor
analogy.story: It actually assigns rooms only when guests arrive and uses empty rooms for storage until needed.
analogy.breaks: Hotels can't share one room between guests; kernels share read-only pages.

code.text:
free -h
#        total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
# Mem:    62Gi   9Gi  1.2Gi  0.5Gi    52Gi        51Gi
# → 51 GiB available; cache is reclaimable

check.q: Which column of free best indicates how much memory applications can still use?
check.a: available, which estimates memory obtainable without swapping, including reclaimable cache.

paging-and-page-tables-the-map.core: Memory is divided into pages (4 KB by default). Each process has a multi-level page table (4 or 5 levels on x86-64) mapping virtual page numbers to physical frames with permission bits (read, write, execute, user/kernel, present, dirty, accessed). The MMU walks it on TLB misses. Page tables enable isolation (no mapping means no access), sharing (several processes map the same frame), copy-on-write, and lazy allocation.

first_principles.problem: An engineer can't explain how two processes can have the same virtual address with different data.
truths: Each process has its own map.

analogy.title: Each tenant's personal building directory
analogy.story: 'Room 101' in your directory may be a different physical room than 'Room 101' in your neighbour's directory.
analogy.breaks: Directories are flat; page tables are multi-level trees.

example.title: Same address, different data
flow: After fork: both → same frame, COW on write

check.q: How can two processes share a library's code without copying it?
check.a: Both page tables map their virtual pages to the same physical frames, marked read-only/executable.

page-faults-when-the-map-fails.core: A page fault happens when an access hits a missing or protected mapping. Minor faults are resolved without disk I/O: first touch of anonymous memory (allocate a zero page), a page already in the page cache, or copy-on-write after fork. Major faults require disk I/O: reading from a file or swapping in. Invalid accesses (unmapped or wrong permission) become SIGSEGV. Major faults are slow (microseconds to milliseconds) and visible as latency.

first_principles.problem: A service has random 50 ms latency spikes correlated with major page faults after memory pressure evicted its pages.

analogy.title: Asking for a book not on your shelf
analogy.story: If it's in the next room (minor), it's quick; if it must be ordered from storage (major), you wait; if it doesn't exist, you get thrown out (segfault).
analogy.breaks: Libraries can lend copies; COW faults create private copies.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Major faults traced to swapped-out heap.

code.text:
ps -o pid,min_flt,maj_flt,cmd -p $(pgrep -o api)
sar -B 1 5           # majflt/s column
perf trace -F maj --pid $(pgrep -o api) -- sleep 10   # which addresses/files

check.q: What's the difference between a minor and a major page fault?
check.a: A minor fault is resolved in memory (e.g. first touch, page cache); a major fault requires reading from disk or swap.

memory-overcommitment-the-calculated-gam.core: Linux lets processes allocate more virtual memory than physically exists, because most allocations are never fully used (sparse arrays, fork before exec, reserved heaps). vm.overcommit_memory 0 is heuristic (the default; refuses obviously excessive requests), 1 always allows, and 2 is strict, limiting commit to swap plus overcommit_ratio% of RAM. Overcommit improves utilisation but means that when everyone does use their memory, something must give: reclaim, swap, or the OOM killer.

first_principles.problem: malloc never fails, yet processes get OOM-killed: the team doesn't understand why allocation succeeded.

analogy.title: Airlines overbooking flights
analogy.story: They sell more tickets than seats because some passengers don't show; occasionally someone gets bumped.
analogy.breaks: Airlines compensate bumped passengers; OOM kills just terminate.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Explains why malloc succeeds but OOM occurs.

code.text:
sysctl vm.overcommit_memory vm.overcommit_ratio
grep -E 'CommitLimit|Committed_AS' /proc/meminfo
# Committed_AS: 180 GB  CommitLimit: 70 GB  (mode 0 allows; risk if all used)

check.q: Why does malloc rarely fail on Linux even when memory is low?
check.a: Overcommit lets the kernel grant virtual allocations without backing them, deferring physical allocation until pages are touched.

swap-the-overflow-parking-lot.core: Swap is disk space where the kernel can move anonymous pages (heap, stack) that aren't file-backed, freeing RAM for active use. A little swap lets the kernel evict cold anonymous pages rather than dropping useful page cache, but heavy swapping of active pages (thrashing) destroys performance. Options include disk swap, swap files, zram (compressed RAM swap) and zswap (a compressed cache in front of disk swap). Kubernetes historically required swap off, with newer versions adding limited support.

first_principles.problem: A server with no swap OOM-kills a process during a short spike, while another server with too much swap becomes unresponsive.
truths: Anonymous pages need somewhere to go.
Disk is far slower than RAM.

analogy.title: An overflow car park
analogy.story: Rarely used cars move to a distant lot, freeing nearby spaces, but if everyone keeps fetching cars from there, traffic grinds to a halt.
analogy.breaks: Car parks don't compress cars; zram compresses pages.

code.text:
modprobe zram && echo zstd > /sys/block/zram0/comp_algorithm
echo 8G > /sys/block/zram0/disksize
mkswap /dev/zram0 && swapon -p 100 /dev/zram0
swapon --show
vmstat 1 5     # watch si/so

check.q: What does sustained high si/so in vmstat indicate?
check.a: Active pages are constantly being swapped in and out (thrashing), meaning the working set exceeds RAM.

swappiness-controlling-the-trigger.core: vm.swappiness (0–200, default 60) sets the kernel's relative preference between reclaiming anonymous pages (by swapping) and file-backed page cache when memory is needed. Low values favour dropping cache and keeping anonymous pages in RAM; high values swap anonymous pages more readily, which suits zram. It doesn't disable swap or set a threshold. Databases often use 1–10; cgroup v2 offers per-cgroup memory.swap.max.

first_principles.problem: A database's buffer pool gets swapped out while the kernel keeps backup file cache in RAM.
truths: Anonymous and file pages have different costs.

analogy.title: Choosing what to put in the attic
analogy.story: You decide whether to store away clothes (anonymous) or books you can re-borrow from the library (file cache).
analogy.breaks: Attics don't decide; swappiness biases kernel reclaim heuristics.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Buffer pool stays resident; cache dropped instead.

code.text:
sysctl vm.swappiness
sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10
echo 'vm.swappiness=10' > /etc/sysctl.d/90-swappiness.conf
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/db.slice/memory.swap.max    # or set 0 for the DB cgroup

check.a: No, it strongly biases reclaim toward file cache, but the kernel can still swap under severe pressure.

the-oom-killer-the-grim-reaper.core: When the kernel can't reclaim enough memory to satisfy an allocation, the OOM killer picks a victim and kills it to free memory. It chooses the process with the highest oom_score, roughly its share of memory (RSS plus swap plus page tables) adjusted by oom_score_adj. In cgroup v2, exceeding memory.max triggers an OOM kill within that cgroup only (container OOMKilled). Logs show the chosen process and memory state.

first_principles.problem: The main database is killed overnight instead of the leaking batch job, because it used the most memory.
truths: Something must be freed when memory runs out.
The biggest consumer is the default victim.

analogy.title: A lifeboat that must lose weight
analogy.story: The captain throws overboard whoever carries the most luggage, unless they're marked essential crew.
analogy.breaks: Captains deliberate; the OOM killer acts in milliseconds by formula.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Batch job becomes the victim next time.

code.text:
journalctl -k | grep -A3 'Out of memory'
# Out of memory: Killed process 4123 (postgres) total-vm:... anon-rss:41GB
for p in $(pgrep -f 'postgres|batch'); do echo "$p $(cat /proc/$p/oom_score) $(cat /proc/$p/comm)"; done
echo -900 > /proc/$(pgrep -o postgres)/oom_score_adj   # protect (prefer OOMScoreAdjust= in unit)

check.q: How does cgroup v2 change OOM behaviour for containers?
check.a: Exceeding a cgroup's memory.max triggers an OOM kill within that cgroup, so only processes in that container are candidates.

influencing-the-oom-killer.core: Shape OOM outcomes deliberately. Set oom_score_adj (−1000 to 1000; −1000 exempts) via systemd OOMScoreAdjust= or Kubernetes QoS classes (Guaranteed pods get low scores, BestEffort high). Contain workloads with cgroup memory.max and memory.high (throttling before OOM). Use userspace killers (systemd-oomd with PSI thresholds, earlyoom) to act earlier and more intelligently. Fix the root cause: leaks, unbounded caches or undersized limits.

first_principles.problem: Kernel OOM happens too late, after the system has thrashed for minutes and become unresponsive.
truths: Kernel OOM is a last resort.

analogy.title: Fire safety rules in a building
analogy.story: Sprinklers in each room (cgroup limits), early smoke alarms (PSI-based oomd), and marking which rooms must never be evacuated last (score adjust).
analogy.breaks: Fires spread physically; memory pressure spreads through shared reclaim.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: DB protected; runaway slices killed early.

check.q: What does cgroup v2 memory.high do differently from memory.max?
check.a: memory.high throttles and reclaims aggressively when exceeded, slowing the workload; memory.max is a hard cap that triggers OOM.

memory-visibility-tools-reading-the-syst.core: The memory toolkit: free -h (available is key), /proc/meminfo (MemAvailable, Cached, Dirty, Slab, AnonPages, Shmem, Committed_AS), vmstat (si/so, free, cache, b), sar -r and -B (history, faults), /proc/pressure/memory (PSI stall time), slabtop (kernel caches), smem and smaps (per-process PSS), and cgroup memory.stat and memory.events for containers. Combine them to tell cache from leak, pressure from usage, and kernel from user memory.

first_principles.problem: A container shows OOMKilled while the node's free memory looks fine.

analogy.title: A doctor's full set of tests
analogy.story: Blood pressure, blood tests and scans each reveal different aspects; diagnosis comes from combining them.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: OOM explained by pod limit, not node memory.

code.text:
cg=/sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod<uid>.slice
cat $cg/memory.max $cg/memory.current
grep -E 'anon |file |shmem ' $cg/memory.stat
cat $cg/memory.events     # oom_kill 3
# limit 512Mi, anon 500Mi → app heap exceeds pod limit

check.q: Why can a container be OOMKilled while the node has free memory?
check.a: The container hit its own cgroup memory limit (memory.max), regardless of node-wide free memory.
